note: Batch 1 broad survey of canonical base feature families across lookbacks to map which effects exist in this panel and in which direction
Batch 2 refine the two live families short horizon 3 to 5 day momentum and 20 day kurtosis plus untested corrm beta and extreme range features
Batch 3 exploit the 1to3 day momentum versus 4to6 day reversal term structure and combine risk normalized momentum with short horizon kurtosis
Batch 4 optimize the two leg and three leg composites of normalized short horizon momentum kurtosis and low beta and check kurtosis lookback plateau

text: Approach so far. Batch 1 mapped base feature families. Findings: this panel shows SHORT horizon momentum (ret(3) SR +0.72, ma(3)/ma(5) negative i.e. price above short MA predicts up) but a REVERSAL at the 4to6 day lag (delay(ret(3),3) SR -0.49). Medium term momentum ret(120) mildly positive +0.59. Volatility, skew, beta and corrm are all weak standalone; beta(120) and corrm(120) negative, consistent with a mild low beta tilt. The strongest orthogonal effect is short window return KURTOSIS: kurt(15) SR +1.10 with a clean plateau across 10/15/20/40 and stable ts_z versions over 60/120/250 windows, which argues it is a real jump/tail premium effect rather than a fitting artifact. Key structural insight: momentum and kurtosis legs are close to orthogonal, so cross sectional z score sums combine them very effectively (1.24 to 1.60) whereas multiplicative combination destroys the signal. Risk normalization of the momentum leg helps consistently: ts_z(ret(3),40) SR +1.03 versus raw ret(3) +0.72, and div(ret(3),std(60)) +0.81. Overfitting control: I am only promoting expressions that sit on a PLATEAU in lookback space rather than isolated peaks, and I prefer composites of few near orthogonal economically motivated legs over deep nested structures. Remaining plan: test third leg candidates and confirm neighbourhood stability before reporting.

text: Final selection reasoning. The panel contains five near orthogonal, economically interpretable effects, each verified to have standalone predictive power in a consistent direction before ever being combined: (1) very short horizon momentum at the 1 to 3 day scale, best expressed risk normalized as ts_z(ret(3), 20 to 60), standalone SR 0.87 to 1.03; (2) a mirror image short horizon REVERSAL at the 4 to 6 day lag, neg(delay(ret(3),3)), standalone SR 0.49, which is why raw ret(5) and ret(10) look dead in aggregate; (3) a strong short window return KURTOSIS or jump premium, peaking around kurt(15) with SR 1.10 and a clean plateau over 10 to 40 day windows and stable ts_z normalizations over 60, 120 and 250 day windows, plus an even better term structure form sub(kurt(15), kurt(40)) at SR 1.20; (4) medium term momentum ret(120), SR 0.59; and (5) a market sensitivity term structure sub(beta(20), beta(120)) and sub(beta(40), beta(250)), SR 0.86 to 1.00, with the related ts_z(corrm(60), 250) confirming the same effect. Combination method: cross sectional z scores summed with equal weights. This was decisively better than multiplicative or ratio combination, which destroyed the signal (mul of two cs_z legs gave SR -0.56), consistent with the legs carrying additive independent information rather than an interaction. Train SR rose monotonically with the number of near orthogonal legs, from 1.10 for the best single feature to roughly 2.0 to 2.2 for seven to ten leg blends. Overfitting control was the central concern given twelve batches and roughly three hundred logged expressions. Three safeguards were applied. First, every leg had to earn its place with a standalone SR of the correct sign, so no leg is a pure curve fitting artifact. Second, I required PLATEAU behaviour rather than isolated peaks: substituting neighbouring lookbacks within any family (momentum 20 vs 40 vs 60, kurtosis 15 vs 20 vs 40, beta 20 vs 60 vs 120 vs 250) moved train SR only within roughly 2.0 to 2.23, a range I treat as noise, which is strong evidence the structure is real. Third, for the final three I deliberately chose blends that ENSEMBLE over parameter choices within a family (two beta lookback pairs, or kurt(15) plus kurt(20) plus its ts_z and term structure forms) rather than the single highest scoring parameterization, and I varied the momentum lookback across the three reported signals so that no single parameter choice is common to all of them. Expected out of sample SR should be materially below the 2.2 train figure because of selection bias, but the diversified additive structure should degrade gracefully rather than collapse.

rationale: All three are equal weight cross sectional z score blends of five near orthogonal effects that each showed standalone predictive power of the correct sign before combination: risk normalized 1 to 3 day momentum (ts_z(ret(3),20 to 40), SR 0.87 to 1.03), the mirror 4 to 6 day reversal (neg(delay(ret(3),3)), SR 0.49), a short window return kurtosis or jump premium in three complementary forms (kurt(15) SR 1.10, ts_z(kurt(15),120) SR 0.99, sub(kurt(15),kurt(40)) SR 1.20), medium term momentum ret(120) SR 0.59, and a market beta term structure (sub(beta(20),beta(120)) SR 0.86, sub(beta(60),beta(120)) SR 0.79), plus short range position maxr(3) SR 0.71. Additive z score combination was decisive: multiplicative combination of the same legs gave SR -0.56, so the legs carry independent additive information. Train SR is 2.23, 2.22 and 2.20 respectively. Selection risk was managed by requiring plateau rather than peak behaviour, since substituting neighbouring lookbacks in any family keeps train SR inside roughly 2.0 to 2.23, and by ensembling over parameter choices within families rather than taking the single best parameterization. The three differ in momentum lookback and in which kurtosis and beta forms are ensembled, so no single parameter choice is shared by all of them.
